subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the statement below.

"The perpendicular force exerted by a surface on an object in contact with the surface."

Which ONE of the following forces is defined by the statement above?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
The normal force is the perpendicular contact force a surface exerts on an object.

subQuestions.questionText:
Two balls of masses m and 2m are dropped simultaneously from the same height above the ground. Ignore air resistance.

When the balls strike the ground, which ONE of the following physical quantities will be the same for both balls?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (2 marks)
Both balls fall freely with the same acceleration from the same height, so they reach the ground with the same velocity. Weight, momentum and kinetic energy all depend on mass and therefore differ.

subQuestions.questionText:
The graph below shows how the momentum (p) of an object changes with time (t). The momentum rises from 0 to about 20 kg·m·s⁻¹ between 0 s and 1 s, stays roughly constant from 1 s to 2 s, then falls steeply through zero to about −20 kg·m·s⁻¹ between 3 s and 4 s.

During which ONE of the following time intervals, measured in seconds, is the magnitude of the net force acting on the object the greatest?
*(Refer to the momentum-time graph in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
Net force equals the rate of change of momentum (gradient of the p-t graph). The steepest gradient, and hence the greatest net force, occurs during the interval 3 s to 4 s.

subQuestions.questionText:
A ball is dropped from a height above a floor. The ball makes an elastic collision with the floor at time t₀ and bounces vertically upwards. Ignore air resistance.

Which ONE of the following graphs shows how the total mechanical energy (E_M) of the ball changes with time?
*(Refer to the four E_M vs t graphs in the original question paper.)*

options.A: E_M is constant, then drops to a lower constant value at t₀.
options.B: E_M remains constant (a horizontal straight line) throughout, including through t₀.
options.C: E_M increases up to t₀ and then stays constant.
options.D: E_M decreases linearly to zero at t₀ and stays at zero.

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (2 marks)
Air resistance is ignored and the collision is elastic, so no mechanical energy is lost. The total mechanical energy remains constant throughout the motion.

subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the two spectrum diagrams below. Diagram 1 shows the line spectrum of an element measured in a laboratory on Earth, with a blue line and a red line at reference positions. Diagram 2 shows the spectrum of the same element from a distant star as observed from Earth, in which the corresponding blue and red lines are shifted towards the red (longer wavelength) end.

Diagram 1 represents the spectrum of an element in a laboratory on Earth. Diagram 2 represents the spectrum of the same element from a distant star as observed from Earth.

Which ONE of the following can be deduced from the spectra above?
*(Refer to the two spectrum diagrams in the original question paper.)*

options.A: The star is moving towards Earth.
options.B: The star is at rest relative to Earth.
options.C: The star is moving away from Earth.
options.D: Both the star and Earth are moving towards each other.

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (2 marks)
The spectral lines are shifted towards the red (longer wavelength). This red shift indicates that the star is moving away from Earth.

subQuestions.questionText:
The diagram below shows the field lines for the combined electric field due to two small charged spheres P and Q. The field lines run from sphere P towards sphere Q.

Which ONE of the combinations below correctly shows the polarity of spheres P and Q?
*(Refer to the field-line diagram in the original question paper.)*

options.A: Sphere P: Negative; Sphere Q: Positive
options.B: Sphere P: Negative; Sphere Q: Negative
options.C: Sphere P: Positive; Sphere Q: Positive
options.D: Sphere P: Positive; Sphere Q: Negative

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
Field lines point away from positive charge and towards negative charge. Lines leaving P and entering Q mean P is positive and Q is negative.

subQuestions.questionText:
Two identical spheres, P and Q, carry charges of +q and −2q respectively. Sphere P exerts an electrostatic force of magnitude F on sphere Q.

Which ONE of the following represents the magnitude of the electrostatic force exerted on sphere P by sphere Q?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (2 marks)
By Newton's Third Law, the electrostatic forces between the two spheres are equal in magnitude. The force on P due to Q equals F.

subQuestions.questionText:
In the circuit diagram shown below all the resistors are IDENTICAL. Ignore the internal resistance of the cell. Voltmeter V1 is connected across the first resistor R1 (in series with the switch and cell), and voltmeters V2, V3 and V4 are connected across resistors arranged so that the current divides among parallel branches.

Which voltmeter will have the HIGHEST reading when switch S is closed?
*(Refer to the circuit diagram in the original question paper.)*
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (2 marks)
Voltmeter V1 reads the potential difference across the single series resistor carrying the full circuit current, which is greater than the potential difference across each resistor in the parallel combination. V1 has the highest reading.

subQuestions.questionText: In which ONE of the following electrical machines is electrical energy converted to mechanical energy?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Generators and dynamos do the reverse.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following combinations correctly links an emission spectrum and an absorption spectrum to the energy transitions of an electron in an atom?

options.A: Emission: from low to high energy levels; Absorption: from high to low energy levels
options.B: Emission: from low to high energy levels; Absorption: from low to high energy levels
options.C: Emission: from high to low energy levels; Absorption: from high to low energy levels
options.D: Emission: from high to low energy levels; Absorption: from low to high energy levels

subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (2 marks)
Emission occurs when an electron drops from a high to a low energy level (releasing a photon); absorption occurs when an electron moves from a low to a high energy level (absorbing a photon).

subQuestions.questionText:
A 20 kg block is placed on a rough surface inclined at 30° to the horizontal. A constant force F, acting parallel to the surface, is applied on the block so that the block moves up the incline at a CONSTANT VELOCITY of 2 m·s⁻¹. A constant kinetic frictional force of 18 N acts on the block. *(Refer to the diagram of the block on the incline in the original question paper.)*

State Newton's First Law in words.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
A body will remain in its state of rest or motion at constant velocity unless a non-zero resultant/net/unbalanced force acts on it. ✓✓
OR
A body will remain in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless a (non-zero) resultant/net/unbalanced force acts on it. ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: Draw a labelled free-body diagram for the block.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks): Accept a force diagram.
Four forces acting on the block, each correctly labelled with an arrow:
• F – applied force, parallel to and up the incline ✓
• N / F_N – normal force, perpendicular to the incline (169,74 N) ✓
• f_k – kinetic friction, parallel to the incline (down the incline, 18 N) ✓
• w / F_g – weight / gravitational force, vertically downwards ✓
Notes: Mark awarded for label and arrow, but penalise only once if arrows are omitted. Do not penalise for length of arrows (not to scale). Any other additional force(s): deduct 1 mark. If force(s) do not make contact with the body: deduct 1 mark.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the magnitude of force F.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks): OPTION 1 (positive up the incline)
F_net = ma
F + f_k + w∥ = ma  ✓ (any one form)
F − (f_k + w∥) = ma
F − [18 + (20)(9,8)(sin 30°)] = 0  ✓ (substitution of f_k ✓ and w∥ ✓)
F = 116 N  ✓
NOTE: F_net = 0, so F = f_k + w∥.

OPTION 2: W_net = ΔE_k
Fx cos 0° + f x cos 180° + w x cos 120° = 0
Fx = 18x + (20)(9,8)x(0,5)
F = 116 N ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
Force F is removed when the block reaches point X on the surface. The block continues to move up the surface and comes to rest momentarily at point Y. Assume that the kinetic frictional force acting on the block remains at 18 N as it moves from point X to point Y.

Write down the net force acting on the block as it moves from X to Y.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks): POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 2.3.
116 N ✓ (= f + w∥) directed down the incline / opposite to the direction of motion ✓
ACCEPT: downwards / down.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the distance between points X and Y.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks): POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 2.4. OPTION 1 (up the incline positive)
F_net = ma
−116 = 20a  ✓
a = −5,80 m·s⁻²
v_f² = v_i² + 2aΔx
0 = (2)² + 2(−5,8)Δx  ✓ (substitution)
Δx = 0,34 m  ✓✓
(Alternatively via v_f = v_i + at giving t = 0,34 s, then x = v_i t + ½at² = 0,34 m.)
OTHER OPTIONS (energy): W_net = ΔE_k
F_net x cos 180° = ½m(v_f² − v_i²)
(116)x cos 180° = ½(20)(0² − 2²)
x = 0,34 m ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
A hot-air balloon is moving upwards at a CONSTANT UNKNOWN speed.

Is the hot-air balloon in free fall? Choose from YES or NO. Give a reason for the answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (2 marks):
No ✓
ANY ONE reason ✓:
• Gravitational force is not the only force acting on the balloon / there are other forces acting on the balloon.
• Its acceleration is not 9,8 m·s⁻² / is zero.
• It has constant velocity / no acceleration.

subQuestions.questionText:
When the balloon is 200 m above the ground, a small stone A is dropped from the balloon. Another small stone B is dropped 5 s later from the balloon while the balloon is still moving upwards at constant velocity. Stone A strikes the ground at a speed of 62,68 m·s⁻¹. Ignore air resistance. *(Refer to the diagram of the balloon 200 m above the ground in the original question paper.)*

Calculate the speed of the hot-air balloon.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks): OPTION 1 (upwards as positive)
v_f² = v_i² + 2aΔy  ✓
(−62,68)² = v_i² + 2(−9,8)(−200)  ✓ (substitution)
v_i = 2,96 m·s⁻¹  ✓
(Downwards positive gives v_i = −2,96 m·s⁻¹ → 2,96 m·s⁻¹.)
OPTION 2 (conservation of mechanical energy): m(9,8)(200) + ½m v² = 0 + ½m(62,68)² → v_i = 2,96 m·s⁻¹. Mass may be omitted during substitution.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the time it takes stone A to strike the ground.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks): POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 3.2.1.
Marking criteria: formula ✓, substitution ✓, final answer 6,70 s ✓ (accept 6,69 to 6,7). The calculation of t for A may be split into two parts.
OPTION 1 (upwards positive):
v_f = v_i + at  ✓
−62,68 = 2,96 + (−9,8)t  ✓
t = 6,70 s (6,698)  ✓
(Downwards positive: 62,68 = −2,96 + 9,8t → t = 6,70 s.)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the distance between the hot-air balloon and stone B at the instant when stone A strikes the ground.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (6 marks): POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTIONS 3.2.1 and 3.2.2.
Marking criteria: formula to calculate y of stone B ✓; substitution of t = 1,7 s (t_A − 5) ✓; substitution to calculate y of stone B ✓; substitution to calculate y of balloon ✓; calculating distance between balloon and stone B ✓; final answer 14,16 m (14,11 to 14,16) ✓.
OPTION 1 (upwards positive):
Stone B: y = v_i t + ½at² = 2,96(6,7 − 5) + ½(−9,8)(6,7 − 5)² = −9,13 m → distance travelled by B = 9,13 m.
Hot-air balloon: y = v_i t + ½at² = 2,96(6,7 − 5) + 0 = 5,03 m → distance travelled by balloon = 5,03 m.
Distance between balloon and stone B = 9,13 + 5,03 = 14,16 m (14,11 − 14,16). ✓
(Relative-velocity method: y = (2,96 − (−2,96))(1,7) + ½(−9,8)(1,7)² gives 14,16 m directly.)

subQuestions.questionText: On the same set of axes, draw position-time graphs for both the hot-air balloon and stone A from the moment the stone is dropped until it strikes the ground. Use the ground as zero reference. Label your graphs BALLOON and A.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks): Criteria for graph:
• Correct shape for stone A, not starting from 0 m. ✓
• Correct shape and initial position for hot-air balloon. ✓
• Gradient for hot-air balloon is higher than that of stone A until stone A reaches its maximum height. ✓
• Both graphs starting at the same position and ending at the same time. ✓
(Stone A rises to a maximum then falls to 0 m; the balloon rises as a straight line from the same 200 m starting position; both begin at t = 0 and end when A strikes the ground.)

subQuestions.questionText:
A ball X, of mass 10 kg, is moving eastwards with a velocity of 2 m·s⁻¹. It collides ELASTICALLY with another ball, Y, of mass 2 kg which was moving with an unknown velocity v_Y (Diagram A). Immediately after the collision, ball X comes to rest and ball Y moves eastwards with a kinetic energy of 36 J (Diagram B). Ignore friction. *(Refer to the before/after collision diagrams in the original question paper; east is positive.)*

Explain the meaning of the term elastic collision.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark. NOTE: if "total" is omitted, minus 1 mark.
A collision in which both the total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved. ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate velocity v_Y.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks): OPTION 1 (conservation of kinetic energy)
E_Ki = E_Kf
½m₁v_i1² + ½m₂v_i2² = ½m₁v_f1² + ½m₂v_f2²  ✓ (any one form)
½(10)(2)² + ½(2)v_iy² = 0 + 36  ✓ (½m_x v_ix² ✓; substitution of 0 and 36 ✓)
v_y = ±4 m·s⁻¹
v_y = 4 m·s⁻¹ west ✓ (accept left)

OPTION 2: from E_Ki = ½m_Y v_f² → v_f = 6 m·s⁻¹, then p_i = p_f: (10)(2) + (2)v_y = 0 + (2)(6) → v_y = −4 m·s⁻¹ = 4 m·s⁻¹ west.

subQuestions.questionText:
The balls were in contact with each other for 0,1 s during the collision.

Calculate the magnitude of the force that ball X exerted on ball Y during the collision.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks): POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 4.2 (for Y; options 1, 3 and 6).
OPTION 1 (east positive), for Y:
F_net Δt = Δp
F_net = m(v_f − v_i)  ✓
F_net(0,1) = 2{6 − (−4)}  ✓ (substitution)
F_net = 200 N  ✓
(Alternatively for X: F_net(0,1) = 10(0 − 2) → F_net = −200 N → magnitude 200 N.)

subQuestions.questionText:
A 2 kg box is released from rest at point P, 5 m above the ground. It slides down a smooth frictionless curved track PQ. *(Refer to the diagram of the track PQR in the original question paper.)*

State the principle of conservation of mechanical energy in words.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark. Accept for isolated system: closed system / only conservative forces act / no external forces act on the system.
The total mechanical energy in an isolated system remains constant / the same. ✓✓
OR
The sum of the kinetic and gravitational potential energies in an isolated system remains constant / the same. ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: Use the PRINCIPLE OF CONSERVATION OF MECHANICAL ENERGY to calculate the speed of the box when it reaches point Q.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks): NOTE: mass may be omitted during substitution. If equations of motion are used, max 1/3 for a correct answer.
OPTION 1:
E_mech(P/top) = E_mech(Q/ground)
(E_p + E_k)P = (E_p + E_k)Q
(mgh + ½mv²)P = (mgh + ½mv²)Q  ✓ (any one form)
(2)(9,8)(5) + 0 = 0 + ½(2)v_f²  ✓ (substitution)
v_f = 9,90 m·s⁻¹ (9,899) ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
The box passes point Q and moves 10 m on a rough horizontal surface before striking a barrier at point R at a speed of 4 m·s⁻¹.

Use ENERGY PRINCIPLES to calculate the magnitude of the average frictional force acting on the box as it moves from Q to R.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks): POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 5.2. OPTION 1:
W_net = ΔE_K
W_N + W_f + W_w = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i²  ✓ (any one form)
f x cos θ = ½m(v_f² − v_i²)
f(10)cos 180° = ½(2)(4² − 9,90²)  ✓✓ (substitution of x cos180° ✓; substitution of v-values ✓)
f = 8,2 N  ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
The barrier exerts an impulse of 14 N·s to the LEFT on the box when the box strikes the barrier.

Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the box after striking the barrier.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks): LEFT NEGATIVE:
F_net Δt = Δp  (accept Impulse = Δmv)
F_net Δt = m(v_f − v_i)  ✓ (any one form)
−14 = 2(v_f − 4)  ✓ (substitution)
v_f = −3 m·s⁻¹  ✓
ΔE_K = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i²  ✓
= ½(2)[(−3)² − 4²]
= −7 J  ✓
(Do not penalise if +3 is substituted.)

subQuestions.questionText:
The siren of a stationary ambulance emits sound waves at a constant frequency of 680 Hz. A man is standing with a detector that records the wavelength of the sound emitted by the siren. The speed of sound in air is 340 m·s⁻¹. *(Refer to the diagram of the ambulance, siren and detector in the original question paper.)*

Calculate the wavelength of the detected sound.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
v = fλ  ✓
340 = 680λ  ✓ (substitution)
λ = 0,5 m  ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
The ambulance now moves at a constant speed along the road TOWARDS the man. The detector now records the wavelength of the sound, which differs from the previous reading by 0,05 m.

State the Doppler effect.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
The change in frequency/pitch/wavelength of the sound detected by a listener because the sound source and the listener have different velocities relative to the medium of sound propagation. ✓✓
OR
An (apparent) change in observed/detected frequency/pitch/wavelength, as a result of the relative motion between a source and an observer (listener). ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: How would the distance between the wave fronts have changed when the ambulance approached the detector compared to when the ambulance was stationary? Choose from INCREASED, DECREASED or NO CHANGE.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark scheme (1 mark): Decreased ✓

subQuestions.questionText: How would the frequency of the detected waves have changed when the ambulance approached the detector compared to when the ambulance was stationary? Choose from INCREASED, DECREASED or NO CHANGE.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark scheme (1 mark): Increased ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the speed of the ambulance.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks): POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 6.1. OPTION 1:
Wavelength approaching = 0,5 − 0,05 = 0,45 m.
f_L = v/λ_L = 340 / 0,45 = 755,56 Hz  ✓ (new wavelength ✓; f_L formula ✓)
f_L = [v / (v − v_s)] f_s
755,56 = [340 / (340 − v_s)](680)  ✓✓ (Doppler formula ✓; substitution ✓)
v_s = 34 m·s⁻¹ (33,67 − 34,04)  ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
A small neutral sphere acquires a charge of −1,95 × 10⁻⁶ C.

Were electrons ADDED TO or REMOVED FROM the sphere?
subQuestions.memoText: Mark scheme (1 mark): Added ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the number of electrons which were added or removed.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks): NOTE: ignore signs of the charges.
n = Q / q_e  ✓
= (1,95 × 10⁻⁶) / (1,6 × 10⁻¹⁹)  ✓ (substitution)
= 1,22 × 10¹³ (1,21875 × 10¹³)  ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term electric field at a point.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
The (electrostatic) force experienced per unit positive charge placed at that point. ✓✓
NOTE (1 mark for): An electric field is a region of space in which an electric charge experiences a force.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the magnitude of the electric field at a point 0,5 m from the centre of the charged sphere.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks):
E = kQ / r²  ✓
= (9 × 10⁹)(1,95 × 10⁻⁶) / (0,5)²  ✓ (substitution)
= 7,02 × 10⁴ N·C⁻¹  ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
Two point charges, q1 and q2, are fixed 0,02 m apart. The magnitude of charges q1 and q2 is the same and q1 is NEGATIVELY charged. The small charged sphere with the charge of −1,95 × 10⁻⁶ C is placed at point P, 0,03 m east of charge q2. The sphere at point P experiences a net electrostatic force of 1,38 N west. *(Refer to the diagram showing q1, q2 and P in a line, with F_E = 1,38 N west, in the original question paper.)*

Calculate the magnitude of the charge on q2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks): OPTION 1. Marking criteria: Coulomb's Law formula ✓; correct substitution for F_q1 OR F_q2 into kQ₁Q₂/r² ✓; correct substitution of 1,38 N for F_net ✓; subtracting (vector addition) the electrostatic forces ✓; final answer 1,11 × 10⁻⁷ C (1,106 × 10⁻⁷ C) ✓.
F_E(net) = F_q2 + F_q1 (magnitudes subtracted, opposite directions)
1,38 = kQ₁Q₂/r² + kQ₁Q₂/r²
1,38 = [(9 × 10⁹)(1,95 × 10⁻⁶)q₂] / (0,03)² − [(9 × 10⁹)(1,95 × 10⁻⁶)q₂] / (0,05)²
q₂ = 1,11 × 10⁻⁷ C (1,106 × 10⁻⁷ C) ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
The battery in the circuit shown below has an emf of 12 V and an unknown internal resistance r. The resistance of the connecting wires and the ammeter is negligible. The circuit contains a resistor X (which dissipates 5,76 W when S is closed) in series between points P and Q, together with a 2,4 Ω resistor and two 6 Ω resistors in parallel; voltmeter V1 is connected across the battery terminals and voltmeter V2 across part of the external network. *(Refer to the circuit diagram in the original question paper.)*

Switch S is OPEN. Write down the reading on Voltmeter V1.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark scheme (1 mark): 12 V ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Switch S is OPEN. Write down the reading on Voltmeter V2.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark scheme (1 mark): 0 (V) ✓

subQuestions.questionText:
Switch S is now CLOSED. The reading on the ammeter is 1,2 A and the power dissipated in resistor X is 5,76 W.

Define the term power.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
The rate at which work is done or energy is expended/transferred. ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the resistance of resistor X.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks): OPTION 1:
P = I²R  ✓
5,76 = (1,2)²R  ✓ (substitution)
R = 4 Ω  ✓
(OPTION 2: P = VI → V = 4,8 V, then R = V/I = 4,8/1,2 = 4 Ω.)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the total EXTERNAL resistance of the circuit.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (3 marks): POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 8.3. OPTION 1:
1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂
1/R_p = 1/6 + 1/8,4  ✓ (the 8,4 Ω is X + 2,4 Ω = 4 + 2,4 in series)
R_p = 3,5 Ω  ✓
R_T = 3,5 + 4 = 7,5 Ω  ✓

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the reading on voltmeter V2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (5 marks): POSITIVE MARKING FROM QUESTION 8.3. Final answer: 3 V.
Step 1 – potential difference across the parallel combination: V_p = IR = (1,2)(3,5) = 4,2 V.  ✓✓ (formula V = IR ✓; substitution ✓)
Step 2 – current in the 8,4 Ω branch: I = V/R = 4,2 / 8,4 = 0,5 A.  ✓ (substitution to calculate I_branch)
Step 3 – V2 across the 6 Ω resistor: V₂ = IR = (0,5)(6) = 3 V.  ✓✓ (substitution ✓; final answer 3 V ✓)

subQuestions.questionText:
A length of wire of negligible resistance is used to connect point P to point Q in the circuit.

How will the reading on voltmeter V1 be affected? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or NO EFFECT. Explain the answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks):
Decreases ✓
• Total resistance decreases. ✓
• Current increases. ✓
• Internal voltage ("lost volts") increases, so external voltage decreases. ✓
NOTE: do not penalise if "total" is omitted.

subQuestions.questionText:
A simplified diagram of an AC generator connected to a 25 Ω resistor is shown below. The coil rotates anticlockwise. *(Refer to the AC generator diagram, with coil sides X and Y between the magnet's N and S poles, in the original question paper.)*

Name the component that distinguishes this generator from a DC generator.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (1 mark): Slip rings ✓
ACCEPT: split ring / slip ring commutator.

subQuestions.questionText: In which direction will the induced current flow in section XY of the coil? Choose from X to Y OR Y to X.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark scheme (2 marks): Y to X ✓✓

subQuestions.questionText:
The graph shows the output voltage of the generator for one cycle of rotation of the coil, with a peak of 100 V and a period of 0,1 s. *(Refer to the output voltage vs time graph in the original question paper.)*

Define the term rms potential difference.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marking criteria (2 marks): If any of the underlined key words/phrases in the correct context is omitted, deduct 1 mark.
The AC potential difference which dissipates the same amount of energy as an equivalent DC potential difference. ✓✓
ACCEPT: The DC potential difference which dissipates the same amount of energy as an equivalent AC potential difference.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the rms current in the circuit.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark scheme (4 marks): OPTION 1:
V_rms = V_max / √2 = 100 / √2 = 70,71 V  ✓✓ (formula ✓; substitution ✓)
I_rms = V_rms / R = 70,71 / 25  ✓ (substitution)
= 2,83 A  ✓
(OPTION 2: I_max = V_max/R = 100/25 = 4 A, then I_rms = I_max/√2 = 4/√2 = 2,83 A.)
